content: Osteoporosis is a condition defined by reduced bone mass and structural deterioration of bone tissue, which leads to increased bone fragility and susceptibility to fractures. In individuals with beta-thalassemia, osteoporosis is a significant cause of morbidity, arising from several underlying mechanisms. Firstly, ineffective erythropoiesis results in bone marrow expansion, which reduces trabecular bone tissue and causes thinning of the cortical bone. Secondly, excessive iron accumulation leads to endocrine dysfunction, which increases bone turnover. Lastly, complications of the disease, such as physical inactivity, further impair optimal bone mineralization. Treatment options for osteoporosis in beta-thalassemia patients include bisphosphonates (e.g., clodronate, pamidronate, alendronate, with or without hormone replacement therapy (HRT)), calcitonin, calcium, zinc supplementation, hydroxyurea, and HRT alone (to address hypogonadism). Denosumab, a fully human monoclonal antibody, works by inhibiting bone resorption and increasing bone mineral density (BMD). Strontium ranelate has a dual mechanism of action, promoting bone formation while simultaneously inhibiting bone resorption, resulting in a net increase in BMD, improved bone strength, and reduced fracture risk. This review aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of treatments for osteoporosis in individuals with beta-thalassemia. The evidence was gathered from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving participants with beta-thalassemia who had a BMD Z score below −2 standard deviations (SDs) for children under 15 years, adult males aged 15 to 50 years, and premenopausal females over 15 years, or a BMD T score below −2.5 SDs for postmenopausal females and males over 50 years. Six RCTs involving 298 participants were included in the analysis. The interventions studied were bisphosphonates (three trials, 169 participants), zinc supplementation (one trial, 42 participants), denosumab (one trial, 63 participants), and strontium ranelate (one trial, 24 participants). The certainty of the evidence ranged from moderate to very low, primarily due to imprecision caused by small sample sizes and methodological concerns such as randomization, allocation concealment, and blinding. Bisphosphonates versus placebo or no treatment: Two trials compared bisphosphonates to placebo or no treatment. One trial (25 participants) found that alendronate and clodronate may increase BMD Z scores at the femoral neck (mean difference (MD) 0.40, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.22 to 0.58) and lumbar spine (MD 0.14, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.23) after two years. Another trial (118 participants) reported that neridronate may increase BMD at the lumbar spine and total hip at six and 12 months, with an increase at the femoral neck observed only at 12 months. The evidence for these findings was of very low certainty. No major adverse effects were reported, and participants receiving neridronate experienced less back pain, which was interpreted as an improvement in quality of life (QoL). However, the certainty of this evidence was also very low. No data were available on BMD at the wrist or mobility outcomes. Different doses of bisphosphonates: One trial (26 participants) compared two doses of pamidronate (60 mg versus 30 mg) over 12 months. The higher dose (60 mg) was associated with greater increases in BMD Z scores at the lumbar spine (MD 0.43, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.76) and forearm (MD 0.87, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.51). No difference was observed at the femoral neck. The evidence was of very low certainty, and the trial did not report fracture incidence, mobility, QoL, or adverse effects. Zinc supplementation versus placebo: One trial (42 participants) found that zinc supplementation probably increased BMD Z scores at the lumbar spine after 12 months (MD 0.15, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.20) and 18 months (MD 0.34, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.40). Similar improvements were observed at the hip after 12 months (MD 0.15, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.19) and 18 months (MD 0.26, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.31). The evidence for these findings was of moderate certainty. However, the trial did not report outcomes related to BMD at the wrist, fracture incidence, mobility, QoL, or adverse effects. Denosumab versus placebo: One trial (63 participants) evaluated denosumab and found low-certainty evidence regarding its effect on BMD Z scores at the lumbar spine, femoral neck, and wrist after 12 months. The trial did not report fracture incidence, mobility, QoL, or adverse effects. However, participants in the denosumab group reported reduced bone pain, as measured on a visual analogue scale, after 12 months (MD −2.40 cm, 95% CI −3.80 to −1.00). Strontium ranelate: One trial (24 participants) reported a narrative increase in BMD Z scores at the lumbar spine in the intervention group, with no corresponding change in the control group. The evidence was of very low certainty. The trial also found a reduction in back pain, as measured on a visual analogue scale, after 24 months in the strontium ranelate group compared to the placebo group (MD −0.70 cm, 95% CI −1.30 to −0.10). This was interpreted as an improvement in QoL. Conclusions: Bisphosphonates may increase BMD at the femoral neck, lumbar spine, and forearm after two years of treatment. Zinc supplementation probably increases BMD at the lumbar spine and hip after 12 months. The effects of denosumab on BMD remain uncertain, and the evidence for strontium ranelate is very limited. Further long-term RCTs are needed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of different bisphosphonates and zinc supplementation in individuals with beta-thalassemia-associated osteoporosis.
